text: The Probability of Backtest Overfitting (PBO) is the probability that the configuration chosen as best in-sample ranks below the median of all N configurations out-of-sample. Bailey, Borwein, Lopez de Prado and Zhu estimate it with combinatorially symmetric cross-validation (CSCV): split the matrix of per-configuration returns into S time blocks, form every half/half train-test combination, and record the out-of-sample rank of the in-sample winner. It needs the return series of every trial. They call the method model-free and non-parametric and say standard hold-out techniques are unreliable and inaccurate for investment backtests. In their examples, higher in-sample SR goes with lower out-of-sample SR, so pushing toward the in-sample optimum becomes detrimental. (high confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: Vendors name survivorship and look-ahead bias as crypto backtest data pitfalls, without quantifying them. CoinAPI: survivorship bias 'occurs when your dataset only includes assets or markets that still exist today', covering delisted pairs, changed symbols, expired derivatives and shut-down venues; its fix is a point-in-time universe rebuilt at each date. Gainium: include failed assets (it cites Bitconnect and OneCoin), and do not alter a finished backtest with information unavailable at the time. Neither gives a number for the effect on returns or drawdown. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: The authors state the limits of their own tools. MinBTL is 'a necessary, non-sufficient condition' and its independent-trials assumption makes it 'quite conservative'. PBO 'does nothing to evaluate the correctness of a backtest': wrong transaction costs or data not available at decision time pass straight through. PBO also cannot see a structural break outside the sample, can be high even when every configuration is skilful, needs disclosure of all trials, and must not be used as an optimization target ('when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure'). The DSR paper says that demanding the trial count 'will not remove the danger completely'. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: Perpetual-futures backtests can omit funding. Gainium says funding fees 'are often neglected, leading to inaccurate representations of profitability' for positions held a long time. Rulyfi's own BTC scan modelled shorts on the price series with no financing (no borrow interest and no perpetual funding) and flags this as a gap between model and venue. Neither source quantifies the error. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: The Deflated Sharpe Ratio paper says the most important information missing from virtually all published backtests is the number of trials attempted, and that a backtest whose search extent was not controlled is 'worthless, regardless of how excellent the reported performance might be'. The long-form Notices paper says published backtests almost never declare the number of trials. An independent open-source lesson makes the same operational point: statistics computed on the selected strategy cannot see the search, so the number of candidates tried must be reported. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: DSR is only as honest as the trial count N. Correlated variants make the effective N much smaller than the literal count: one simulation found a 275-variant moving-average sweep behaved like about 10 independent trials (average pairwise correlation 0.65). The same source says the estimate is specific to that grid. A crypto backtest vendor states that the true number of trials behind its indicator search is probably larger than the 95.1 million it counted, so its luck bar is likely understated. An understated N makes DSR optimistic. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: Surviving strategies in that search traded only 30 to 63 times, so skew and kurtosis estimates, which DSR depends on, are noisy. DSR on small trade counts inherits that noise. (low confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe

text: Two complementary multiple-testing adjustments exist for Sharpe ratios. DSR benchmarks against the extreme-value expectation of the best of N trials and needs N, trial-Sharpe variance, skew, kurtosis and T. The Harvey-Liu haircut converts the Sharpe into a t-ratio and p-value, adjusts the p-value for multiple tests with Bonferroni, Holm or BHY using an assumed number of prior tests and a user-set correlation level, and converts back into a haircut Sharpe. The DSR paper says Harvey and Liu's threshold plays an analogous role to its own and encourages computing DSR with both. (medium confidence)
keywords: Backtest pitfalls overfitting and deflated Sharpe
